drafts.title: $0. That's what a new Medicare card costs. AI makes the fake call sound real (AP5, AI for normal people / scams / 55+)
drafts.window: Tue ~11 AM-12 PM MT (very strong Tuesday cell).
drafts.angle: Medicare Open Enrollment started Oct 15. The "your new card is in the mail, just verify your number" call is the classic, and Medicare's own security team says AI now makes those callers sound friendly, local and accent-free. Give older folks and their kids one rule they'll remember. The honest side of AI for the masses: the tool isn't scary, the crooks using it are. Sat's VA fake-grant item never went live, so it rides along as the second example.
bullets: Medicare Open Enrollment runs Oct 15 to Dec 7, 2026 (Medicare.gov).
Medicare cards are free, and Medicare won't call, text or email out of the blue asking for your Medicare number, Social Security number or bank info (Medicare.gov).

CMS security blog: AI lets scammers write natural scripts in real time, remove accents, and personalize calls by age and benefits. One mother-in-law gave her Medicare number on a "new card" call before a back-brace pitch tipped her off.
What to do: hang up, call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) or the number on your card. A handy exit line: "My son told me to hang up."
Same week: VA News (Oct 13-14) warned about a fake, official-looking "Veterans & Retired Seniors Grant" ad that got vets to hand over direct-deposit info.
Pixel: 20 sec talk-to-camera at home: "If someone calls about your new Medicare card, hang up. It's free and they already have your number."
Premium reply/quote: AARP Fraud Watch Network or a big senior-finance account posting about Open Enrollment this week. One line with the hang-up rule and 1-800-MEDICARE.
drafts.body:
SHORT VERSION:
$0. A new Medicare card is free, and Medicare won't call you to "verify" your number.

Open Enrollment just started, and AI makes these calls sound friendly and local now.

Hang up and call the number on your card.

[my take: ___]

Who in your family needs to hear this?

LONGER VERSION:
If you're on Medicare, or your mom or dad is, read this one.

Open Enrollment started Oct 15. That's when the "new Medicare card" calls ramp up. Someone friendly says your new card is on the way and they just need to verify your number.

Medicare's own security people say AI is making these calls harder to spot. The caller sounds local, has no accent, and seems to know your age and your benefits.

Here's the truth: a new Medicare card is free. Medicare won't call out of the blue asking for your Medicare number, your Social Security number or your bank info.

Our family rule:
1. Nobody shares a number on a call they didn't make.
2. Hang up and call 1-800-MEDICARE or the number on the back of your card.
3. You're allowed to be rude. "My son told me to hang up" works fine.

VA warned vets about the same trick this week with a fake grant ad.

[my take: ___]

Who in your family needs to hear this?

drafts.window: Mon ~1-2 PM MT (strongest cell, gives three days before Thursday's vote). Backup Wed ~1-3 PM MT.
drafts.angle: A tiny, concrete bill number with a vote this week. Keep it to who pays and let the audience argue it. No politics, no reactor specs. This is the one SMR item this week (replaces the held TVA Clinch River item).
bullets: Louisiana Public Service Commission vote scheduled Thursday, Oct 22, on the "Louisiana Advanced Nuclear Exploration" program (The Center Square via American Press, Oct 16, 2026).
As proposed, utilities could add 20 cents a month to customer bills, about $4 million a year across the three big investor-owned utilities.
The money would fund feasibility studies, site checks, cost modeling and early licensing prep for small modular reactors and microreactors.
Proposed amendment (Commissioner Eric Skrmetta): let utilities spend up to $2 million and ask to recover it in rates later instead.
Commissioner Davante Lewis supports more nuclear but says it "should not happen on the backs of ratepayers."

drafts.body:
SHORT VERSION:
20 cents a month.

That's what Louisiana regulators may add to power bills to study small nuclear reactors. The vote is Thursday.

Would you pay 20 cents a month for that, or should the power companies foot the bill?

LONGER VERSION:
20 cents a month. That's the number on the table in Louisiana.

On Thursday the state's utility regulators vote on letting power companies add about 20 cents a month to customer bills. Across the big utilities that's about $4 million a year.

The money wouldn't build anything yet. It pays for studies: where small reactors could go, what they'd cost, and early paperwork with federal regulators.

One commissioner wants the companies to spend up to $2 million first and ask to get it back later. Another says he's for nuclear, just not "on the backs of ratepayers."

I think small reactors could mean steadier bills for families down the road. [my take on who should pay: ___]

So I'll ask you. Would you pay 20 cents a month for that, or should the power companies foot the bill?
